sources.text: Two years ago, the students of a city secondary school turned the empty roof of their building into a small vegetable garden. At first, the project was meant to be a one-term science activity. However, the garden soon became a popular place to spend break time, and a group of students offered to water the plants during the summer holiday. Today, the school kitchen uses some of the vegetables, and younger classes visit the roof to learn how plants grow. The teacher who started the project says the biggest surprise was not the harvest but the number of students who kept coming back without being asked.

sources.title: Let Us Sleep: Why Our School Day Should Start Later
sources.author: Imagined student writer (invented)
sources.rights_note: Tự soạn cho khóa học (Pilot Kit B v0.2.1); người viết, trường, thành phố và mọi con số là giả định. Không chép từ đề thi hay ấn phẩm nào.
sources.text:
¶1 Every morning at 6:15, my alarm goes off, and every morning I make the same promise: tonight I will go to bed earlier. I never do. I am not lazy, and neither are my classmates. The problem is that our school day starts at 7:00, which is simply too early for teenagers. I believe our school should move the start of lessons to 8:00.

¶2 My first reason is health. Doctors often explain that during the teenage years the body clock shifts, so many teenagers do not feel sleepy until late in the evening. If we have to get up before 6:30, we cannot get the eight to ten hours of sleep that we need. Last month, the student council asked 200 students in our school about their sleep. Sixty-two per cent said they slept fewer than seven hours on school nights.

¶3 My second reason is learning. Anyone who has visited a first-period class knows what I mean: half the room is yawning, and the other half is staring at the board without seeing it. A tired student is not a stupid student, but he or she is a slower one. Starting an hour later would turn that wasted first lesson into a useful one.

¶4 Third, a later start would make mornings safer. At the moment, many of us cycle to school in the dark during the winter months, when the roads are busy with trucks.

¶5 Some people argue that a later start means a later finish, so students would have less time for homework and extra classes. That is true, but it misses the point. An extra hour in the afternoon is worth much less than an extra hour of sleep. In any case, students who sleep longer will be more alert in the evening too, so they will finish their homework faster.

¶6 Changing the timetable will not be easy. Teachers, parents and bus drivers would all need to adjust. But if we really care about students, the question is not whether we can afford to change. It is whether we can afford not to.

sources.author: Imagined student-council speaker (invented)
sources.rights_note: Tự soạn cho khóa học (Pilot Kit B v0.2.1); người viết, trường, thành phố và mọi con số là giả định. Không chép từ đề thi hay ấn phẩm nào. Phát bằng giọng đọc máy cố định trên máy phụ huynh; không ghi âm giọng Nguyên.
sources.text:
Good morning, everyone. I'm speaking on behalf of the student council about our proposal to put water refill stations in the school. At the moment, our canteen sells about three hundred plastic bottles of water every day, and most of them end up in the bin after one use. We think there is a better way.
Our plan is simple. The school would put three refill stations in the main building, and every student would be asked to bring a reusable bottle. The stations would cost money at the start, but the canteen would no longer need to order bottled water, so the cost could be recovered in about two years.
Of course, there are some concerns. Some parents have asked whether the water would be safe to drink. That's a fair question, and we think the filters should be tested every term, with the results posted on the notice board. Others worry that younger students will forget their bottles. For them, the canteen could keep a small supply of paper cups.
We are not saying this will solve every environmental problem. But it is a practical step, and we'd like to try it for one term and then review it together.

sources.title: The planning fallacy
sources.author: Pilot Kit B author
sources.rights_note: Tự soạn cho khóa học (Pilot Kit B v0.2.1); người viết, trường, thành phố và mọi con số là giả định. Không chép từ đề thi hay ấn phẩm nào. KHÔNG cho thầy/cô xem trước buổi (FIXLIST #1).
sources.text: Most people are surprisingly bad at predicting how long their own tasks will take. Psychologists call this the "planning fallacy". When we plan, we tend to imagine the best version of the task: we picture ourselves working steadily, with no interruptions, no mistakes and no tiredness. We rarely think about the things that went wrong last time. Interestingly, when we predict how long other people's tasks will take, we tend to be less optimistic, because we think about what actually happened to them before rather than about their hopes. One way to reduce the planning fallacy is to ask, "How long did a similar task actually take me last time?" and to use that answer, not your hopes, as a starting point. Another tip is to break a big task into smaller steps and estimate each one, which makes it harder to forget parts of the work.

sources.title: Short Blocks, Long Results (exam-style reading)
sources.author: Pilot Kit B author
sources.rights_note: Tự soạn cho khóa học (Pilot Kit B v0.2.1); người viết, trường, thành phố và mọi con số là giả định. Không chép từ đề thi hay ấn phẩm nào.
sources.text:
¶1 Many students sit down to do their homework with good intentions and stand up three hours later wondering where the time went. One reason is that the brain finds it hard to stay focused on a single task for a long period. Phones, snacks and conversations offer easy escapes, and every interruption makes it harder to return to the work.

¶2 A simple method that many students find useful is to divide study time into short blocks. In each block, you work on one task for about twenty-five minutes, with your phone in another room. Then you take a five-minute break to stretch, drink some water or look out of the window. After four blocks, you take a longer rest.

¶3 The method works for several reasons. First, a short block feels manageable, so it is easier to start. Second, because you know a break is coming, you are less tempted to stop in the middle. Third, counting the blocks gives you a realistic picture of how long a task really takes, which helps you plan the next day.

¶4 However, the method is not magic. Some tasks, such as writing an essay, need longer periods of deep concentration, and a timer that rings in the middle of a good idea can be annoying. Students who use the method successfully tend to adapt it: they make the blocks longer for creative work and keep them short for tasks they find boring, such as memorising vocabulary.

¶5 The most important lesson may be that how you study matters as much as how long you study. Two focused hours can achieve more than four distracted ones.

sources.text:
¶1 Last week I kept a diary of my evenings. On Monday I had homework in five subjects, and I finished at 11:40 p.m. On Wednesday it was 11:15. My friends say their weeks look the same. In a quick poll I ran in our class, 27 of 35 students said they regularly do more than three hours of homework a night.

¶2 This is not sustainable. Teenagers need time to sleep, to exercise and simply to talk to their families. When every evening is filled with worksheets, we stop learning and start copying, just to get the work done.

¶3 I am not asking for homework to be abolished. Some practice is useful, especially before tests. But each teacher sets work as if their subject were the only one. A limit of ninety minutes a night, shared fairly between subjects, would force teachers to choose the tasks that really matter. Quality, not quantity, should be the rule.

sources.text:
¶1 Every year, some students tell me they have too much homework. I take that seriously. But a strict time limit is the wrong answer.

¶2 First, students work at very different speeds. A task that takes one student twenty minutes can take another an hour. A fixed limit would punish the slower students, who often need the practice most.

¶3 Second, homework is where much of the learning actually happens. In class, students watch me solve problems; at home, they find out whether they can do it alone. Last year, students in my two classes who completed at least 80 per cent of their homework scored, on average, 1.2 points higher in the end-of-year test than those who did not.

¶4 Of course, that does not prove that homework caused the difference; the students who did their homework may simply have been more motivated. Still, I believe the real problem is badly designed homework, such as long, repetitive worksheets, not homework itself. Teachers should coordinate across subjects and set fewer but better tasks.

sources.text:
¶1 When Linh's class teacher suggested a "phone-free week", most of the class laughed. Linh, who is fifteen, admits that she used to check her phone more than a hundred times a day, often without noticing. "It was like a reflex," she says. "I would pick it up just because it was there."

¶2 The rules of the challenge were simple. Students could keep a basic phone for calls and messages to their families, but there would be no social media, games or videos for seven days. Anyone who gave up could rejoin the next day, with no punishment.

¶3 The first two days were the hardest. Linh kept reaching into her pocket for a phone that was not there, and she felt anxious that she was missing important news from her friends. By Wednesday, however, something had changed. She noticed that she was finishing her homework earlier, and she had started reading a novel she had abandoned months before. "I wasn't cleverer," she says. "I just had fewer interruptions."

¶4 Not every student had the same experience. Of the thirty-two who started, eleven gave up before the end of the week, and some said the challenge made them feel left out, because their friends in other classes were still chatting online without them.

¶5 At the end of the week, the class discussed what they had learned. Few students wanted to give up their smartphones permanently. Instead, many decided to set their own rules, such as leaving the phone outside the bedroom at night. Linh's rule is simple: no phone until her homework is finished. "I still love my phone," she says. "I just don't want it to be the boss."

¶1 Four weeks ago, our school became phone-free. Students now hand in their phones at the gate in the morning and collect them at 4:30 p.m. I want to thank parents for supporting this important change.

¶2 The results so far are encouraging. Break times are noisier and happier: students are finally playing football and table tennis again instead of staring silently at screens. Most importantly, reports of online bullying to our school counsellor fell from nine in the month before the ban to two in the first month after it.

¶1 Every time a school bans phones, adults celebrate. But a full-day ban treats every student as someone who cannot control themselves, and it takes away a useful tool.

¶2 Last week, we asked readers of this blog how they use their phones at school. Of the 80 students who replied, 64 said they use them for dictionaries, timetables or contacting their parents after clubs. Banning phones all day makes these simple things harder.

¶3 It is also too early to say that bans stop bullying. Bullying does not disappear when phones are locked away at 7 a.m.; it can simply move to the evening, when teachers cannot see it.

¶4 Schools should teach responsible use instead: phones away in lessons, allowed at break, and clear consequences for misuse. That is how we will learn to manage technology as adults.

sources.title: The Bicycle Bus (exam-style reading)
sources.author: Pilot Kit B author
sources.rights_note: Tự soạn cho khóa học (Pilot Kit B v0.2.1); người viết, trường, thành phố và mọi con số là giả định. Không chép từ đề thi hay ấn phẩm nào.
sources.text:
¶1 In some cities, a new kind of "bus" has started to appear on the roads on weekday mornings. It has no engine, no driver and no ticket machine. It is a bicycle bus: a group of children who cycle to school together, guided by a few adult volunteers.

¶2 The idea works like an ordinary bus route. The group follows a fixed path and stops at the same corners at the same times, where more children join. By the time it reaches the school gate, a bicycle bus may have grown from five riders to fifty. Because the children ride as one large, visible group, drivers slow down and give them space, which makes many parents feel more comfortable about letting their children cycle.

¶3 Supporters say the benefits go beyond safety. Children arrive at school awake and in a good mood after twenty minutes of exercise. Fewer cars near the school gate mean less traffic and cleaner air for everyone. And for many children, the ride is simply the most enjoyable part of the day.

¶4 Bicycle buses are not without difficulties, however. They depend entirely on volunteers, and when a key parent moves away or changes jobs, a route can disappear. They also work best where the roads are reasonably flat and where at least some cycle lanes exist. In cities with heavy traffic and no safe space for bikes, organisers warn that a bicycle bus should not be started without support from the local authorities.

¶5 Even so, the idea is spreading, largely because it is cheap: all it needs is bicycles, a route and a few adults who are willing to get up early.

sources.title: Source A — Free Rides for Those Who Need Them Most
sources.author: Imagined retired teacher, local newspaper column, October 2026 (invented)
sources.rights_note: Tự soạn cho khóa học (Pilot Kit B v0.2.1); người viết, trường, thành phố và mọi con số là giả định. Không chép từ đề thi hay ấn phẩm nào. Lanford và Westbrook là thành phố giả định. Nguồn dùng cho bài nói Chủ nhật: thầy/cô KHÔNG đọc trước.
sources.text:
¶1 Our city likes to say that its buses are "for everyone". But for many people, they are not. A monthly bus pass in Lanford costs 300,000 dong. For a student or a pensioner, that is a lot of money, and for a family with three children at secondary school it is almost a million dong a month.

¶2 The city has a limited budget for public transport, and it must decide how to spend it. I believe the fairest choice is to make buses free for students, people over sixty and low-income workers. These are the people who depend on buses most, because they cannot afford cars or taxis. In the neighbouring city of Westbrook, where fares for students were removed two years ago, school attendance rose and fewer teenagers rode motorbikes without a licence.

¶3 Some will say that free rides are a gift the city cannot afford. But a city that wants clean air and safe roads cannot afford to keep its poorest residents off the bus.

sources.title: Source B — A Bus That Never Comes Is Not Cheap
sources.author: Imagined urban-planning student, Lanford public city forum, October 2026 (invented)
sources.rights_note: Tự soạn cho khóa học (Pilot Kit B v0.2.1); người viết, trường, thành phố và mọi con số là giả định. Không chép từ đề thi hay ấn phẩm nào.
sources.text:
¶1 Cheaper fares sound fair, but they miss the real problem. On most routes in Lanford, buses come only every 25 to 30 minutes, and they are often late. If you have to wait half an hour, even a free bus is not much use, especially in the rain.

¶2 According to the city transport office's own estimate, removing fares for students, older people and low-income workers would cost about the same as doubling the number of buses on the ten busiest routes. In the office's passenger survey last year, 58 per cent of passengers named waiting time as their biggest complaint; only 21 per cent named the price.

¶3 Better service helps everyone, including the poorest passengers, who often have the longest journeys. Of course, some families genuinely cannot afford the fare, and they should get help. But the city's main investment should go into frequency: a bus every ten minutes would bring more people onto public transport than any discount.

sources.author: Pilot Kit B author
sources.rights_note: Tự soạn cho khóa học (Pilot Kit B v0.2.1); người viết, trường, thành phố và mọi con số là giả định. Không chép từ đề thi hay ấn phẩm nào.
sources.text:
¶1 When cheap pocket calculators first appeared in shops, many teachers were alarmed. If a machine could do arithmetic in a second, they asked, why would any child bother to learn their times tables? Some schools banned calculators completely. Others allowed them only in the final years of secondary school.

¶2 Over time, a more balanced view developed. Most teachers today agree that students still need to understand how numbers work and to be able to estimate an answer in their heads. Without this understanding, a student who presses the wrong button will not notice that the answer is ridiculous. At the same time, the calculator frees students from long, repetitive calculations, so they can spend more time on the reasoning behind a problem.

¶3 The lesson from this debate is not that every new tool is harmless, nor that every new tool is a threat. Rather, it is that a tool changes what we need to learn. When calculators arrived, mental arithmetic became less important for getting exact answers but more important for checking whether an answer made sense.

¶4 Today, a similar debate is taking place about chatbots that can write essays and explain homework in seconds. Some people fear that students will stop thinking for themselves; others see a tireless personal tutor. If the history of the calculator is any guide, the answer will depend less on the tool itself than on the rules and habits that grow up around it. Students who use the tool to check and extend their thinking are likely to benefit; those who use it to avoid thinking are not.

sources.text:
¶1 I used to dread maths homework. If I got stuck at ten at night, there was nobody to ask: my parents were tired, and my tutor only comes on Saturdays. This term, I started using an AI chatbot, and it has changed everything.

¶2 I never ask it for the answer. Instead, I type in my working and ask it where my mistake is, or I ask it to explain a step in a different way. Sometimes I ask it to give me three similar problems so I can practise. I use it for about thirty minutes, three evenings a week. My maths test scores went from 6.5 at the start of the term to 8 in the mid-term test.

¶3 A chatbot is like a patient tutor who never gets tired. Banning AI completely would be pointless, because students will use it anyway. Schools should teach us to use it well: ask for explanations, not answers.

sources.title: Source B — When the Machine Writes, Who Learns?
sources.author: Imagined English teacher, school newsletter for parents, October 2026 (invented)
sources.rights_note: Tự soạn cho khóa học (Pilot Kit B v0.2.1); người viết, trường, thành phố và mọi con số là giả định. Không chép từ đề thi hay ấn phẩm nào. Nguồn dùng cho bài nói Chủ nhật: thầy/cô KHÔNG đọc trước.
sources.text:
¶1 This term I noticed that several homework essays in my grade-9 class were suddenly fluent, well organised and strangely similar. When I asked, some students admitted they had used a chatbot to write a first draft.

¶2 So I tried a small comparison. Of the 36 students in the class, 14 said they had used a chatbot for their essays during the previous month. In an in-class essay test, written without any devices, those 14 students scored on average 1.5 points lower than the others.

¶3 I must be careful here: students chose for themselves whether to use the chatbot, and those who did may have been weaker writers to begin with. It is one class over one month. But the pattern worries me. When the machine does the thinking, the student just copies, and chatbots will make lazy students lazier.

¶4 I am not calling for a ban. Students may use AI to check grammar or explain a word after they have written their own draft. But the first draft must be theirs.
